name: work-on
description: 'Starts, continues, or logs project work: finds or creates the work item, works out where it stands, and runs its next step through to a built result. Use when the owner asks to build, add, fix, or change something, says "keep going" or "continue", names an item, or wants an idea logged for later.'

# Work on

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: the work plugin's `references/conventions.md` (saving, section edits, history, branches) and `references/trackers.md`, two folders above this skill's folder (`../../references/`). To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line: in Codex a command joined by `&&`, `;`, a pipe, or a heredoc, or run from a script, runs inside the sandbox and fails. Give text with `--text`, or a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder (never a fixed `/tmp` name, deleted right after the command). Never change a record with a script.

## Steps

1. No session briefing in this conversation: run the command below. Exit code 4 (no `.toolkit.json`): open `project-setup` and stop. When the briefing or a `toolkit work` command lists changes found in the tracker (a moved or renamed folder, a new parent, a missing item), tell the owner each one in one line before other work.
   `toolkit brief`
2. Find the item: the id the owner named, or a title in the list that matches the request. Two possible matches: ask one question naming both. No match: it is new. When `PROJECT-ROADMAP.md` names the item, read its phase there too.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
   `toolkit work list`
3. Size a new request. Setup is not a work item: never create one for setup steps; owner steps go in the reply and in the current focus under "Waiting on the owner". "New work", "track", "work item", or "done properly" always makes an item, and content the owner has not described is a question for him, never a quick edit. A quick edit (one sitting, no choice for the owner, no behavior recorded in `requirements/`, nothing bound for production): do it and report it, with no item. "Later", "backlog", "park that": check the list for a duplicate, create the item, write the owner's words unchanged into Starting request, reply "Logged as WI-014 (bug, backlog). Not started." and stop. Anything else: create it the same way, titled in the owner's words (say the title in one line), and continue.
   `toolkit work new --title "<title>" --type <type> --stage 01-discovery`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Starting request" --text "<the owner's words>"`
4. A substantial goal whose item shows `delivery: not-offered`: open `work-delegate` first. When it asks the offer, wait for his answer before building. Quick questions and small edits get no offer.
5. Route by where the item stands, using the item and the "Continue with" column of the lifecycle. Requirements not approved and type `build` or `data-load`, or the owner answered the questions that set them, or asked for it done properly: `work-requirements`, which shows them to him for approval. More than one reasonable way to build it and no approved design: `solution-design`. A `build` item going to planning without a design: say so in the final reply, not a progress line ("One way to build this: <approach>. I'll build it that way; say 'design first' to stop me."), and put the reason in a history note. An item that changes committed files goes through stage 07 (its own worktree), never onto the default branch. Too big for one build: `work-organize`. Stages 09 to 11: `work-check`. Stages 12 to 14: `work-finish`. `waiting_on: owner`: ask that one question first (`work-decide`) and keep working on anything it does not block. Say the route in one line ("WI-012 is waiting for your OK on the requirements; opening work-requirements."). Never ask the owner which stage it is in.
   `toolkit work lifecycle`
6. Plan (stage 06): Roadmap phases `P1`, `P2` and tasks `P1-T01` (Work, Deliverable, Done when, Depends on) from the design's "Build and verification plan", in the table and checkbox format in this skill's own `references/planning.md` (the `references/` folder beside this `SKILL.md`; read it first). Tracking setup (stage 07) only when needed: the item's worktree `.claude/worktrees/wi-<number>-<slug>` on branch `claude/wi-<number>-<slug>`; in a Salesforce project, the item's folder in `delivery/deployment/` through `sf-component-tracker`.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 06-implementation-plan`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section Roadmap --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section Tasks --set-file <file>`
7. Build (stage 08) on the item's own branch and worktree, never on the default branch. In Codex, `git worktree add`, `git add`, and `git commit` need the owner's approval and escalated permissions (`sandbox_permissions` set to `require_escalated`, with a one-line reason), because the sandbox keeps `.git/` read-only: say in one line what each does before Codex asks. Refused without asking: show him the exact command, ask him to approve it or run it in a terminal, and set the item waiting on the owner. Never work around it (the work plugin's `references/conventions.md`, "Branches and worktrees"). With a team recorded by `work-delegate`: one `builder` agent per independent task, one writer per path. Tests go with each task. Tick a task only with evidence. A task whose "Done when" names the owner is a question for him (step 8). Salesforce: `sf-component-tracker` on each metadata change; production data only through `sf-data-change`.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 08-build`
8. When the owner is needed: add an Open Questions row (next free `Q-` number) with "owner" as who decides, set the item waiting on the owner, keep working on tasks that do not depend on the answer, and tell him in one line. After his last answer, set it back to the agent (`../../references/conventions.md`, "Waiting on the owner").
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --append-row "| <next Q-id> | <question> | <affects> | Open | owner |"`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
9. Last task done: open `work-check`. This skill never records approvals, Done, merges, or deploys.
10. Before stopping with work unfinished: Overview (Current position, Next action) and Notes > Resume here are current, one history note says what changed, and validation is clean. End the reply with the one question for the owner, or the exact words that continue ("Say 'keep going' and I'll build P1.").
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "<what changed>"`
   `toolkit work validate <id>`

## Agents

- `builder`: one per independent build task, only when `work-delegate` recorded a team or the owner agreed to one. The main agent merges each builder's branch into the item's branch, then ticks the task.
- `researcher`: one per unknown found while planning or building.
- `acceptance-checker`: a plan check after step 6, before the build, when the plan has several builders, parallel tasks, or a shared environment. Paste in the requirements, the design's "Build and verification plan", the Roadmap, and the Tasks, and ask for a plan check.
- How to brief them: `../../references/helpers.md`.
- Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Read the agent's file in this plugin's `agents/` folder and give its full text, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. With no worker, do the work yourself and say that no independent check ran.

## Sizing a request

- **Quick edit, no item:** one sitting, no decision for the owner, and it does not change behavior recorded in `requirements/`. Examples: fix a typo, rename a variable, answer a question. Report what changed in one line.
- **Log only:** the owner says "later", "backlog", "park that", "not now", or "log a bug". Create the item at `01-discovery`, fill Starting request with his exact words, and stop. Do not start the work.
- **Work item:** everything else. A request that grows past a quick edit while you work on it becomes an item then, with the owner's words as the Starting request.
- Types: pick the closest from the lifecycle's type list. `build` and `data-load` need approved requirements before stage 03 is passed; the CLI refuses otherwise. A change to what the product does, to Salesforce metadata (`force-app/`), or to anything bound for production is `build` (data changes are `data-load`), never `task`, even when it looks small.

## Routing notes

- The lifecycle's "Continue with" column is the default. The item's real state decides: for example, a `task` type item with no open choices can skip requirements approval and go straight to planning, with the reason in a history note.
- Stages may be skipped, repeated, or revisited. Record a short reason when a move is not obvious.
- A worktree whose branch names an item (`claude/wi-<number>-<slug>`) belongs to that item. The briefing says so. Work on that item there.
- Several items at once: recommend what can proceed independently, what depends on another outcome, and which decision would unblock the most work. See this skill's own `references/planning.md`.
- `PROJECT-ROADMAP.md` holds the project's phases (`P01`) and deliverable-sized work units, each naming its work item ID; item detail stays in the tracker. A new item that is one of those units gets its ID written into the unit, saved with `publish-docs`. An item's own phases (`P1`) are a different thing and live in its Roadmap section.

## Never

- Never record an approval, Done, or a cancel here. Those belong to `work-requirements`, `solution-design`, `work-check`, `work-decide`, and `work-finish`.
- Never merge, deploy, or write production data.
- Never create a second tracker or a local copy of items kept in Notion, GitHub, or Jira.

# Work decide

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: the work plugin's `references/conventions.md`, two folders above this skill's folder (`../../references/conventions.md`). To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line: in Codex a command joined by `&&`, `;`, a pipe, or a heredoc, or run from a script, runs inside the sandbox and fails. Give text with `--text`, or a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder (never a fixed `/tmp` name, deleted right after the command). Never change a record with a script.

## Steps

1. Build the queue: requirements waiting for approval, designs marked proposed, items at stage 11 waiting for result approval, and Open Questions rows where the owner decides. The command lists each decision once. Its "Agent to-do" lines are the agent's own steps, not decisions waiting on the owner: count and show only the decisions, and handle a delivery offer there with `work-delegate` after the queue.
   `toolkit work decisions`
2. The owner gave an answer without being asked ("approved", "go with B"): match it to exactly one waiting decision. If two could match, ask which one, naming both.
3. Otherwise take the decisions one at a time, the one blocking the most work first. For each: what is being decided, the choices, your recommendation and its main reason, and what happens after each answer. Every decision carries a recommendation, even when it is the only one in the queue; a bare question is not enough. One decision per message.
4. A requirements approval: save his words as a history note first, so no later session asks him again. Then check the Agreed goal and the open questions. The goal still holds the template text: write the goal he was shown with the approval question, then record the approval. A requirement still has an open question linked: say which one, open `work-requirements` for it, and record the approval, without asking him again, once it is answered.
   `toolkit work show <id> --section Requirements`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "Owner's words: <quote>" --effect "Requirements approval to record."`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Agreed goal" --text "<goal he was shown>"`
5. Record each answer where it belongs. Approvals (for requirements, first set each approved `R-xx` Status to Finalized and put who approved it and when in its Decision record, as `work-requirements` step 8 does; after it, a `build` or `data-load` item goes to `solution-design` unless the owner agreed to skip the design, and a skip is said in the final reply). A design approval also answers an open question that asked for that choice: mark that row Answered.
   `toolkit work approve <id> --requirements --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work approve <id> --design --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work approve <id> --result --by <owner>`
   An Open Questions answer: rewrite that row with the answer, the date, and status Answered.
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --set-file <file>`
   Then, for an approval or an answer: one history note in the owner's words (a requirements approval has it from step 4), and `waiting_on` set to `agent` when the agent continues (the approve command sets it to `none` by itself), unless another question for him on that item is still open.
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "Owner's words: <quote>"`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
   A delivery offer listed as an agent to-do: open `work-delegate` once the owner's decisions are done.
6. A decision for the whole project: add a `DECISIONS.md` row and save it with `publish-docs`. Run the command inside the worktree `publish-docs` opens, then let it commit and push.
   `toolkit decision add --decision "<decision>" --why "<why>" --by <owner>`
7. A "no" or a change: record it as the answer, move the item back (for example to refinement), and open the skill that redoes the work.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 02-refinement`
8. Lead with "Not saved" if any write failed. When the queue is empty, say so and offer to continue unblocked items with `work-on`. End the reply with the next decision's question, or the exact words that continue.

## What counts as an answer

- Only the owner's explicit words count. Quote them in the history note. The lifecycle command prints the full approval rules:
  `toolkit work lifecycle`
- A question, a suggestion, a tentative answer ("probably B"), or silence is not an answer. Ask again in one line.
- An approval covers only what was shown. It never covers merge, deployment, spending, or publishing.
- "Yes", "ok", or "looks good" with nothing waiting: ask what he is approving.
- Set `waiting_on` to `agent` when the agent can continue, to `none` when nothing waits, or keep `owner` when another owner question is still open on that item.

## After a result approval

The item continues with `work-finish` (pull request, deployment, requirements baseline, Done). Open it when the owner wants it shipped now.

## Project-wide decisions

- A decision for the whole project goes in `DECISIONS.md`, not in memory and not in one item. Examples: "use Postgres everywhere", and a standing merge instruction ("agents may merge a pull request after an independent check finds no blocking issue").
- A decision that replaces an older one names it with `--replaces D-<n>`:
  `toolkit decision add --decision "<decision>" --why "<why>" --by <owner> --replaces D-<n>`
- A decision about one item stays in that item: its Recent History, the answered Open Questions row, and Notes > Decisions and context when the next session needs the context.
- `DECISIONS.md` is append-only. Never rewrite or remove a row; a changed decision is a new row that names the one it replaces.

## Tracker notes

- GitHub Issues or Jira: the `toolkit work` commands exit with code 3. Build the queue from the waiting-on-owner and stage 11 labels that `../../references/trackers/github.md` or `../../references/trackers/jira.md` names, and record answers as `../../references/trackers.md` says. Remove the waiting-on-owner label after each approval or last answer, as above.

# Work check

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: the work plugin's `references/conventions.md` and `references/helpers.md` (how to brief agents), two folders above this skill's folder (`../../references/`). To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line: in Codex a command joined by `&&`, `;`, a pipe, or a heredoc, or run from a script, runs inside the sandbox and fails. Give text with `--text`, or a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder (never a fixed `/tmp` name, deleted right after the command). Never change a record with a script.

## Steps

1. Read the requirements, the acceptance list, and the tasks, then set the testing stage. When the show output's "Design:" value is not `none`, also read the design's Acceptance checks (in "Build and verification plan") and the selected option's "How to check it" column (the design command exits 1 for an item with no design). A sub-item whose "Design:" says "none of its own" and names its parent's approved design is checked against that design: read the parent's.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
   `toolkit work design <id>`
   `toolkit work design <parent-id>`
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 09-testing`
2. Run the project's tests and every acceptance check the item lists. A check with several scenarios or manual steps gets a test plan: a copy of `tests/TEST-PLAN-TEMPLATE.md` named for the item, with the results filled in. A check that could not run is reported as not run, never as passed.
3. Brief the `acceptance-checker` agent (never the agent that built it): one verdict per requirement (met, partly met, not met) with evidence, plus defects seen in the diff. Give it the branch and commit to check.
4. Failures: set the bug-fixing stage; a `builder` agent (or the main agent) fixes; the checker checks again. Repeat until clean, or until a failure needs an owner decision (an Open Questions row and the item waiting on the owner).
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 10-bug-fixing`
5. Record the result: what was checked, the evidence, the known gaps.
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "Checked: <what>; evidence: <where>; gaps: <gaps or none>"`
6. Set the approval stage and wait on the owner. Show him what it does now, how to see it (a link, a command, or a screenshot), the evidence, and the gaps. Ask one line: "Do you approve this result?"
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 11-user-approval --waiting-on owner`
7. Yes: record it (the command adds its own history row), quote his words in one note, and hand the item back to the agent unless another question for him is still open; then open `work-finish`. A requirement change goes to `work-requirements`; a fix becomes a task and continues here. Every reply ends with the approval question, or the exact words that continue.
   `toolkit work approve <id> --result --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "Owner's words: <quote>"`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`

## Agents

- `acceptance-checker`: step 3 and every re-check. Paste in the Agreed goal, every `R-xx` with its acceptance check, the Acceptance list, the design's Acceptance checks and "How to check it" column, and the test plan when there is one. Name the branch and commit.
- `builder`: fixes in step 4 when a team was recorded or the owner agreed; one builder per independent fix, one writer per path.
- Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Read the agent's file in this plugin's `agents/` folder and give its full text, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. With no worker, do the work yourself and say that no independent check ran.

## Showing the result

- Lead with what the result does now, in the owner's terms: "The export button now creates a CSV file that opens in Excel."
- Then how he can see it himself: the link, the command to run, or a screenshot.
- Then the evidence: tests run and their result lines, the checker's verdicts.
- Then the gaps: anything partly met, not run, or known to be missing. Never hide a gap to get an approval.
- One question: "Do you approve this result?"

## Rules

- The checker is independent: never the agent or session that built the change. When no independent check could run, say so plainly before asking for approval.
- A check that did not run is never reported as passed.
- The approval covers the result shown. It is not an approval to merge, deploy, or publish; `work-finish` handles those.
- "Looks good" to a question other than the approval question is not the approval. Ask the approval question.
- A "no": record his words, turn each named problem into a task or a requirement change, and continue.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. Change the stage label and record the result in the issue as `../../references/trackers.md` says.

# Conventions every work skill follows

Every skill in the work plugin follows these rules. A skill's own `SKILL.md`
names the file when a rule matters for a step.

This file is `references/conventions.md` in the work plugin's own folder. From
a skill's `SKILL.md` it is two folders up: `skills/work-on/SKILL.md` and
`references/conventions.md` share the plugin folder. In Codex the plugin
folder is the installed copy, for example
`~/.codex/plugins/cache/toolkit-v2/work/<version>/`, so this file is
`~/.codex/plugins/cache/toolkit-v2/work/<version>/references/conventions.md`.

Four rules that are easy to miss:

- Run each `toolkit` command alone, as its own command (below).
- Never change a work item with a script (Python, Node, `sed -i`, `cat >`).
  Use `toolkit work edit --section` or `--label`, or the file edit tool for
  body text. The hooks refuse the script, so it only wastes a step.
- Temporary text goes in `--text`, or in a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder,
  never at a fixed name such as `/tmp/wi001.md`.
- End every reply to the owner with the one question he must answer, or with
  the exact words that continue the work ("Say 'keep going' and I'll start the
  build."). Never end on "The next step is ..." with nothing for him to do.

## Voice

Every skill carries this line near its top:

> Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.

Agents do not receive the output style. Each agent file in `agents/` carries
its own writing rules.

## Opening another skill

- Claude Code: use the Skill tool with the skill's name, for example
  `work-requirements`.
- Codex: read that skill's `SKILL.md` from the path shown in the skill list,
  then follow it.
- Say the handover in one line, for example "WI-012 needs a design; opening
  solution-design."
- The skill that asked a question records the answer. An answer that arrives
  later, after that skill has finished, is recorded by `work-decide`.

## Running `toolkit` commands

- Put each `toolkit` command on its own line and run it as a plain command.
  Do not wrap it in `$(...)`, a pipe, or a redirect. Codex matches its
  command rule against the plain command. This holds for read commands too:
  `toolkit work decisions && toolkit work show WI-001` is two commands.
- In Codex, a `toolkit` command joined to anything else (`&&`, `;`, a pipe, a
  heredoc, `cd ... &&`) or run from a script (for example Python's
  `subprocess`) runs inside the Codex sandbox. The sandbox blocks Notion,
  Hindsight, and the main checkout's `.work-items/` and `.memory/` from a
  worktree, so the command fails or reports the wrong cause. Run each one
  alone, as its own command.
- Add `--json` when you need to read the output field by field.
- Exit codes: `0` done; `1` error; `2` validation failure (fix what it names
  and run it again); `3` not supported for this tracker or memory backend
  (follow [trackers.md](trackers.md)); `4` not a Toolkit V2 project (open
  `project-setup`).
- "saved but not verified" in the output means the write happened and the
  read-back failed. The message names the first line that differs. Lead the
  reply to the owner with "Saved but not verified", say which line, and read
  the item back to judge it.

## Changing a work item

- Change a work item only through `toolkit work` commands. This keeps the
  local tracker and Notion the same, and it keeps the CLI's record of what it
  wrote. A value the agent changes by hand looks like an owner edit to the
  CLI.
- Find a file only with the command below. Never build a path by hand: the
  owner may have moved or renamed the folder.

  ```text
  toolkit work show <id> --path
  ```

- To change one section of the body, read it, change only what needs to
  change, and write the whole section back. The file holds the same text the

# Image Generation Skill

Generates or edits images for the current project (for example website assets, game assets, UI mockups, product mockups, wireframes, logo design, photorealistic images, or infographics).

## Top-level modes and rules

This skill has exactly two top-level modes:

- **Default built-in tool mode (preferred):** built-in `image_gen` tool for image generation, editing, and transparent-image requests. Does not require `OPENAI_API_KEY`.
- **Fallback CLI mode:** `scripts/image_gen.py` CLI. Use when the user explicitly asks for or confirms the CLI/API/model path. Requires `OPENAI_API_KEY`.

Within CLI fallback, the CLI exposes three subcommands:

- `generate`
- `edit`
- `generate-batch`

Rules:
- Use the built-in `image_gen` tool by default for normal image generation and editing requests.
- Do not switch to CLI fallback for ordinary quality, size, or file-path control.
- For transparent images, ask built-in `image_gen` for a transparent background and preserve the generated alpha.
- Never silently switch from built-in `image_gen` or CLI `gpt-image-2` to CLI `gpt-image-1.5`; ask the user first unless they explicitly requested `gpt-image-1.5`.
- The word `batch` by itself does not mean CLI fallback. If the user asks for many assets or says to batch-generate assets without explicitly asking for CLI/API/model controls, stay on the built-in path and issue one built-in call per requested asset or variant.
- If the built-in tool fails or is unavailable, tell the user the CLI fallback exists and that it requires `OPENAI_API_KEY`. Proceed only if the user explicitly asks for that fallback.
- If the user explicitly asks for CLI mode, use the bundled `scripts/image_gen.py` workflow. Do not create one-off SDK runners.
- Never modify `scripts/image_gen.py`. If something is missing, ask the user before doing anything else.

Built-in save-path policy:
- In built-in tool mode, Codex saves generated images under `$CODEX_HOME/*` by default.
- Do not describe or rely on OS temp as the default built-in destination.
- Do not describe or rely on a destination-path argument (if any) on the built-in `image_gen` tool. If a specific location is needed, generate first and then move or copy the selected output from `$CODEX_HOME/generated_images/...`.
- Save-path precedence in built-in mode:
  1. If the user names a destination, move or copy the selected output there.
  2. If the image is meant for the current project, move or copy the final selected image into the workspace before finishing.
  3. If the image is only for preview or brainstorming, render it inline; the underlying file can remain at the default `$CODEX_HOME/*` path.

- Extending or matching an existing SVG/vector icon set, logo system, or illustration library inside the repo
- Creating simple shapes, diagrams, wireframes, or icons that are better produced directly in SVG, HTML/CSS, or canvas
- Making a small project-local asset edit when the source file already exists in an editable native format
- Any task where the user clearly wants deterministic code-native output instead of a generated bitmap

## Decision tree

Think about two separate questions:

1. **Intent:** is this a new image or an edit of an existing image?
2. **Execution strategy:** is this one asset or many assets/variants?

Intent:
- If the user wants to modify an existing image while preserving parts of it, treat the request as **edit**.
- If the user provides images only as references for style, composition, mood, or subject guidance, treat the request as **generate**.
- If the user provides no images, treat the request as **generate**.

Built-in edit semantics:
- Built-in edit mode is for images already visible in the conversation context, such as attached images or images generated earlier in the thread.
- If the user wants to edit a local image file with the built-in tool, first load it with built-in `view_image` tool so the image is visible in the conversation context, then proceed with the built-in edit flow.
- Do not promise arbitrary filesystem-path editing through the built-in tool.
- If a local file still needs direct file-path control, masks, or other explicit CLI-only parameters, use the explicit CLI fallback only when the user asks for it.
- For edits, preserve invariants aggressively and save non-destructively by default.

Execution strategy:
- In the built-in default path, produce many assets or variants by issuing one `image_gen` call per requested asset or variant.
- In the CLI fallback path, use the CLI `generate-batch` subcommand only when the user explicitly chose CLI mode and needs many prompts/assets.
- For many distinct assets, do not use `n` as a substitute for separate prompts. `n` is for variants of one prompt; distinct assets need distinct built-in calls or distinct CLI `generate-batch` jobs.

Assume the user wants a new image unless they clearly ask to change an existing one.

## Workflow
1. Decide the top-level mode: built-in by default, including transparent-output requests; fallback CLI only if explicitly requested or confirmed.
2. Decide the intent: `generate` or `edit`.
3. Decide whether the output is preview-only or meant to be consumed by the current project.
4. Decide the execution strategy: single asset vs repeated built-in calls vs CLI `generate-batch`.
5. Collect inputs up front: prompt(s), exact text (verbatim), constraints/avoid list, and any input images.
6. For every input image, label its role explicitly:
   - reference image
   - edit target
   - supporting insert/style/compositing input
7. If the edit target is only on the local filesystem and you are staying on the built-in path, inspect it with `view_image` first so the image is available in conversation context.
8. If the user asked for a photo, illustration, sprite, product image, banner, or other explicitly raster-style asset, use `image_gen` rather than substituting SVG/HTML/CSS placeholders. If the request is for an icon, logo, or UI graphic that should match existing repo-native SVG/vector/code assets, prefer editing those directly instead.
9. Augment the prompt based on specificity:
   - If the user's prompt is already specific and detailed, normalize it into a clear spec without adding creative requirements.
   - If the user's prompt is generic, add tasteful augmentation only when it materially improves output quality.
10. Use the built-in `image_gen` tool by default.
11. For transparent-output requests, ask built-in `image_gen` for a transparent background and preserve the generated alpha channel.
12. Inspect outputs and validate: subject, style, composition, text accuracy, and invariants/avoid items.
13. Iterate with a single targeted change, then re-check.
14. For preview-only work, render the image inline; the underlying file may remain at the default `$CODEX_HOME/generated_images/...` path.
15. For project-bound work, move or copy the selected artifact into the workspace and update any consuming code or references. Never leave a project-referenced asset only at the default `$CODEX_HOME/generated_images/...` path.
16. For batches or multi-asset requests, persist every requested deliverable final in the workspace unless the user explicitly asked to keep outputs preview-only. Discarded variants do not need to be kept unless requested.
17. If the user explicitly chooses or confirms the CLI fallback, then use the fallback-only docs for model, quality, size, `input_fidelity`, masks, output format, output paths, and network setup.
18. Always report the final saved path(s) for any workspace-bound asset(s), plus the final prompt or prompt set and whether the built-in tool or fallback CLI mode was used.

## Prompt augmentation

Reformat user prompts into a structured, production-oriented spec. Make the user's goal clearer and more actionable, but do not blindly add detail.

Treat this as prompt-shaping guidance, not a closed schema. Use only the lines that help, and add a short extra labeled line when it materially improves clarity.

### Specificity policy

Use the user's prompt specificity to decide how much augmentation is appropriate:

- If the prompt is already specific and detailed, preserve that specificity and only normalize/structure it.
- If the prompt is generic, you may add tasteful augmentation when it will materially improve the result.

Allowed augmentations:
- composition or framing hints
- polish level or intended-use hints
- practical layout guidance
- reasonable scene concreteness that supports the stated request

Not allowed augmentations:
- extra characters or objects that are not implied by the request
- brand names, slogans, palettes, or narrative beats that are not implied

The fallback CLI defaults to `gpt-image-2`.

- Permission-set assignments are org data. The package installs `Account_Tier_Edit` but does not assign it to users. Manual assignments may diverge from profile membership after a user update.

**Access and security**

- Inventory profiles of all users who can view Account, including users whose Account access comes from a permission set. Give each such profile read access to `Account.Tier__c` in Setup. Keep field edit off those profiles except System Administrator.
- Set `Account.Tier__c` read and edit permissions on `Account_Tier_Edit`. Assign it only to active users whose current profile is Sales Manager. Audit assignments against the current active Sales Manager user list at release and after every membership change. Remove assignments when a user leaves the profile; add one when an active user joins. Manual review does not enforce the rule during the interval between a profile change and assignment update. Salesforce's documented User Access Policies may grant and remove permission sets on user create or update using profile criteria in supported editions. Verify availability, exact criteria, actions, ordering, and profile-entry and profile-exit behavior in this target org before treating that as a dependable mechanism.
- Audit all other permission sets, permission set groups, and profiles for `Tier__c` edit grants. Remove or avoid grants that would let another profile's user edit. Salesforce permissions add together; a read-only profile setting does not cancel another edit grant.
- Field edit access does not replace Account object edit permission or record-level access. Use test Accounts that the Sales Manager and System Administrator users can edit. Verify real profile names and user assignments. Enumerate and test every distinct effective profile, permission-set, and permission-set-group combination among Account viewers, including users with multiple grants.

**Integrations**

- No integration or automation is requested. API clients can read the field only if their Salesforce user has Account and field read access. An update needs Account and field edit access plus record access.

**Operations**

- Deploy the field, permission set, and approved view metadata through the work-item package to the sandbox. Configure profile field permissions in Setup after the field exists. Assign `Account_Tier_Edit` to active Sales Manager users and test a dependable profile-tied assignment process. Record profiles, assignments, the effective-access matrix, and manual release steps for the owner. Agents do not deploy to or change production.
- Review assignments whenever users join or leave the Sales Manager profile. Recheck baseline read and unwanted edit grants when a profile or permission set changes Account access. This option has ongoing assignment work.

#### Tradeoffs and risks

| Tradeoff or risk | Effect and response |
| --- | --- |
| Manual `Account_Tier_Edit` assignments do not follow profile membership at the moment it changes. | A missed addition blocks an approved user; a missed removal leaves an unwanted edit grant. Option B is conditional and not recommended on manual assignments alone. Verify a supported, configured User Access Policy or another dependable mechanism in the target org and test both profile entry and exit before selecting it. |
| Profile baseline read and System Administrator edit settings are manual and absent from source control. | Record Setup steps and verify them in each target org. The metadata package alone does not complete access configuration. |
| Permissions from profiles and permission sets add together. | Another edit grant could break R-01. Audit every route to field edit access, then test a non-manager Account viewer. |
| The exact position of Rating in `Account Layout` is not yet verified. | Retrieve the layout, insert Tier immediately after Rating in the same column, and review the diff and rendered record. |
| Account viewers may have different layout assignments or Dynamic Forms pages. | Inventory every affected assignment and verify Tier directly below Rating in each actual view. Stop for scope correction if approved changes cannot achieve this. |
| The repository has no `force-app` source today; sandbox field existence is unresolved. | Inspect sandbox `Tier__c` first. Reuse or adjust it if present, or add it if absent. |

#### Build order

1. Inspect sandbox `Account.Tier__c` existence; inventory Account-viewing profiles, every effective permission combination, Sales Manager users, all affected Account layout and Lightning page assignments, Dynamic Forms, and `Account Layout`. Check User Access Policy availability and existing policies. Depends on sandbox read access. Complete when field status, access matrix, assignments, and Rating's actual position are recorded. Stop for scope correction if approved view changes cannot give every affected viewer the required placement.
2. Add or adjust `Account.Tier__c` custom field metadata with the approved values, order, optional setting, no default, description, and help text. Depends on step 1. Complete when metadata review shows every field setting without a duplicate field.
3. Add `Account_Tier_Edit` permission set metadata with field read and edit for `Account.Tier__c`, and no added Account object access. Depends on step 2. Complete when permission-set metadata contains only the intended permissions.
4. Add Tier directly below Rating on `Account Layout` and each other approved assigned view that needs it; create a narrow work-item package manifest. Depends on steps 1 to 3. Complete when diffs preserve unrelated content and every affected view can show the required placement.
5. Validate and deploy the narrow package to the sandbox using its alias from `.toolkit.json`. Depends on step 4. Complete when Salesforce accepts the metadata and the field appears on the intended layout. Do not target production.
6. Configure baseline field read on every Account-viewing profile and field edit on the System Administrator profile in sandbox Setup. Keep edit off other profiles. Assign `Account_Tier_Edit` only to active Sales Manager profile users. Audit all edit grants. If User Access Policies are available, configure profile-based grant and removal actions for the permission set and verify their action order and triggers; otherwise mark Option B unable to guarantee R-01 and do not recommend it. Depends on step 5. Complete only when assignments and effective grants match the approved rule and the target-org mechanism is verified.
7. Test saving Gold, Silver, Bronze, and blank as Sales Manager and System Administrator users. Verify read and edit for every affected profile and permission-set or group combination, including denied API edits for every non-manager combination. Test profile entry and exit and confirm the permission-set grant and removal take effect as needed. Check Tier below Rating in every actual assigned Account view. Depends on step 6. Complete only when R-01 is observed for the full affected set and assignment transitions.
8. Prepare the owner's production release instructions with the narrow package, manual profile settings, tested assignment mechanism, permission audit, and verification steps. Depends on step 7. # Permission Sets in Git

A permission set retrieve is complete since API 40.0. A permission set deploy replaces the whole component: any grant missing from the file is disabled.

- Bring a permission set into git only with `permsets.py fetch <Name> --org <sandbox>`. Never commit a file that did not verify clean.
- Before relying on retrieves in a new org or after a major release, run `permsets.py verify` on one large permission set.
- Fetch fresh before every edit.
- Before every deploy, run `permsets.py preflight <file> --org <sandbox>`. `sf project deploy validate` and `sf project deploy preview` cannot detect removed grants.
- A preflight receipt expires after 30 minutes. Re-run it before the deploy.
- To remove grants on purpose, re-run the preflight with `--accept-removals`.
- Deploy to a sandbox only, with the owner's yes in the same chat. The owner runs production.
- Never use `--ignore-conflicts` on a permission file.
- Keep `sourceApiVersion` in `sfdx-project.json` equal to the org's version. Re-fetch everything after a version bump.
- Before committing, run `permsets.py check`, then `permsets.py tidy`.
- After every fetch, re-add the grants in `RETRIEVE_BLIND_SPOTS`.
- After a deploy, check every permission set group that contains the set. If its status is not Updated, click Recalculate on the group in Setup.
- Never hand-merge a git conflict in a permission file. Take one side whole, then re-apply the other change.
- Never write an `Activity.` field permission. Use `Task.` or `Event.`.
- Profiles are excluded. Never deploy a profile from source.
- Never edit or disable `.claude/hooks/guard-permission-set-deploy.cjs`. If the hook matches quoted text in another command, put the text in a file.

Procedures and reasons: `tools/permissions/PERMISSIONS-RUNBOOK.md` and `tools/permissions/permsets.py`.

# Publish a documentation save

Save an agreed change to Git-tracked project documents from its own temporary
worktree, and push it straight to the default branch with no pull request.
The project's rule for this is `.claude/rules/publish-project-documents.md`;
its `paths` list names the documents this skill saves.

1. **Confirm it is documentation in an allowed path**, not code, rules, skills,
   hooks, settings, `.memory/`, or `.work-items/` (list below).
2. **Start a save workspace** from the project, with the script in the
   `scripts/` folder beside this `SKILL.md`:

   ```text
   node <this skill's folder>/scripts/publish-docs.mjs start --branch <default-branch> -- <file> [more files]
   ```

   It fetches the remote, creates a separate sparse worktree beside the project,
   and prints its path. Work only in that path for this save.
3. **Make the edit there and stage the files by name.** Read the full staged
   diff. Add `DECISIONS.md` rows only with `toolkit decision add`, run there.
   After a change under `ai-external-knowledge/`, regenerate its index there
   ("Step 3 in detail") and stage `ai-external-knowledge/INDEX.md` too.
4. **Publish** from the save workspace:

   ```text
   node <this skill's folder>/scripts/publish-docs.mjs publish --message "<plain commit message>"
   ```

   It refuses other staged paths, unstaged or untracked files, and conflict
   markers (trailing spaces are fine: two make a Markdown line break); commits;
   pushes without force; and checks the remote has the commit.
5. **Report** the commit id and that it reached the remote. After the task's
   last publish, remove the clean save workspace (`git worktree remove <path>`).

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.

Codex: its sandbox keeps `.git/` read-only, so every Git write here (the script's `start` and `publish`, `git add`, `git commit`, `git push`, `git worktree add` and `remove`) needs the owner's approval and escalated permissions. Run each one as its own command with `sandbox_permissions` set to `require_escalated` and a one-line reason saying what it does; an approval without escalation still runs inside the sandbox and fails on `.git/index.lock`. When Codex refuses a command without asking ("approval required by policy"), stop, show the owner the exact command, and ask him to approve it in an interactive session or run it in a terminal. With no remote (`git remote` prints nothing), skip `git fetch`.

## What counts as documentation

The project documents are the paths in the project's
`publish-project-documents.md` rule. The script accepts only these:

- Files under `requirements/`, `system-guide/`, `ai-external-knowledge/`, and
  `delivery/` of these document types: `.md`, `.txt`, `.csv`, `.xml`, `.png`,
  `.jpg`, `.jpeg`, `.gif`, `.svg`, `.pdf` (for example
  `delivery/deployment/component-tracker.csv` and a `package.xml`). A
  `.gitignore` file under `delivery/` is also accepted. `delivery/` exists
  only in Salesforce projects.
- `DECISIONS.md`, `PROJECT.md`, and `PROJECT-ROADMAP.md` at the project root,
  and `tools/permissions/PERMISSIONS-RUNBOOK.md` in a Salesforce project.
- `README.md` files.

It refuses:

- Every file under `delivery/data/` except `.md` notes and `.gitignore`,
  whatever `.gitignore` says. Load files and backups there can hold production
  records and personal data, and `.gitignore` there lists only some file types.
- Any other file type: code (`.js`, `.mjs`, `.py`, `.sh`, `.cls`, `.trigger`),
  settings, `.json`, spreadsheets.
- Hidden files and folders, such as `.env` or `.github/`.
- `.memory/` and `.work-items/`. They are local and Git-ignored; change them
  only through `toolkit memory` and `toolkit work` commands.
- Instruction files (`AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `SKILL.md`) anywhere, in any
  letter case.
- Any path Git ignores.

A folder or a `.md` extension alone does not make a file documentation. Rules,
skills, prompts, hooks, settings, and code change behavior: they use a worktree
and a pull request. Documentation that cannot be separated from a code change
stays with that change and its review. Do not split dependent changes to avoid
review, and do not describe an unshipped feature as shipped.

This skill changes how a save is published, not who may change the content.
Saving requirements or a design does not approve them or their build.

## Step 1 in detail: choose the exact files

Confirm the repository, the default branch, the remote, and the Git identity
that will publish. Name every file in the save. Look at existing local edits
first; never take another session's uncommitted work or overwrite it.

When this session already made the edit in its working checkout, carry it
across: start the save workspace, copy each edited file into the same path
there, stage, and publish. After the publish is verified, return this
session's own copy in the working checkout to its committed state
(`git restore -- <file>`, only for files this session edited). The published
version comes back with the next `pull-latest`, which would otherwise stop on
the changed file.

## Step 3 in detail: the knowledge index and decision rows

`ai-external-knowledge/INDEX.md` is generated. Never edit it by hand. In the
save workspace, run:

```text
toolkit index knowledge
```

Then stage the regenerated `ai-external-knowledge/INDEX.md` with the files you
changed. The script allows that file in any save that touches
`ai-external-knowledge/`.

`DECISIONS.md` rows are written by `toolkit decision add`, run in the save
workspace. It assigns the next id. Never type a row by hand.

Check links and formatting in the other documents you changed. A failed check
or an unexpected staged path leaves the save unfinished. Never bypass a failing
check.

## Recover without losing work

- The default branch advanced: bring this save workspace current (fetch, then
  rebase or merge onto `origin/<default-branch>` inside the save workspace
  only), regenerate the knowledge index if the save touches it, rerun the
  checks, and run `publish` again. A refused push does not touch any other
  checkout. Ask the owner only when the meaning of the change or who approved
  it changes.
- The default branch advanced and both sides added `DECISIONS.md` rows: take
  the remote's `DECISIONS.md`, then run `toolkit decision add` again for this
  save's rows, so each gets the next free id. Never renumber the other rows.
- A refused push, an account mismatch, a login prompt, a protected branch, a
  conflict, or a failed check: report separately what is written, checked,
  committed, and published. Keep the save workspace, any commit id, and the
  exact next action in the work item or the handoff.
- Never force-push, bypass branch protection, retry through another account,
  reset, or stash another session's work. An unpushed commit is unfinished.
- Reuse the same save workspace only while a follow-up save to the same files
  is still pending in this task. Do not delete another session's save
  workspace.

# Salesforce deploy hitch-hiker check

A metadata deploy ships the whole current source of every component it names, not only your edit. A hitch-hiker is a component in the deploy set, or an undeployed edit inside a named component's file, that would land in the target org although it is not the intended change or its feature is not ready there.

Two shapes:
1. A whole component the target does not have yet. The deploy creates it. Example: a field whose LWC, Apex, page, or backfill has not shipped.
2. Extra edits inside a file you touch for one reason. Example: you change a field's help text; the deploy also ships a renamed label, a new rollup filter, a changed formula, or added picklist values in that file.

## When to run

- Before every deploy to a shared or higher org, by `-x`, `-m`, or `-d`.
- Before you give the owner any production deploy command.

## The check

1. List the exact deploy set: every `<members>` in the `-x` manifest, every member in the `-m` list, every file or folder under `-d`. An `-x` deploy of a full-cutover manifest is the highest risk. Check the whole member list.
2. For each named component, the whole current `force-app/` definition ships: label, inline help text, formula, rollup and summary filters, picklist values, all field metadata, and the component itself if the target lacks it.
3. For each component, decide whether its feature is already live in the target. Hitch-hiker signals:
   - The component tracker (if the project keeps one) marks it as not in the target org.
   - It belongs to a work item or feature the owner has not called ready for that org.
   - The file has edits beyond the intended one. Diff it against the last deployed commit, or run `git log` on the path.
   - When `tools/kb/` exists, run `python tools/kb/query_graph.py <Object.Field>` to see what the component connects to. A connected component that is not in the target org is a candidate hitch-hiker.
4. Treat any tracker as a hint, not proof. Before you call a component missing, verify against the target org read-only: `sf sobject describe`, or a SOQL or Tooling query for the field, class, or flag. Do not block a deploy on a stale tracker alone. Do not tell the owner something rides into production until a read-only check confirms it is not already there.
5. If a confirmed hitch-hiker remains, stop. Do not deploy. Do not hand over the command. Tell the owner which component, what would ship, and why it may be unintended. The owner decides: narrow the deploy set, or confirm the rider is wanted.

## Narrow the deploy set

- Name only the components the change needs. For a help-text change on three fields, name those three fields, not a broad manifest.
- Naming a component still ships its whole file. Run the per-file diff in step 3 on a narrow deploy too.
- Prefer the work item's `package.xml` over `delivery/deployment/full-project-deployment-template/package.xml` unless the goal is a full cutover.

## Why the check ends with an org read

A tracker can be stale in either direction. In one real case a help-text deploy was suspected of carrying a new field, label renames, and a rollup filter to production. A read-only production check showed they were already live. The mechanism is real; the tracker was wrong.

## Related

- `salesforce-org-safety.md`: the read-only verify in step 4 is allowed there.
- `sf-component-tracker` skill: the tracker this check reads.
- The production-org guard hook asks before a production deploy runs. This check runs before that prompt.

# Salesforce component tracker

Keep the deployment records current in the same response as the change.

A project that already uses `engagement/` uses `engagement/deployment/` wherever this skill says `delivery/deployment/`. Do not create a parallel `delivery/` tree. A project with another artifact root keeps these records where it stores deployment records.

## Deployment folder

```
delivery/deployment/
  component-tracker.csv                  one tracker for the whole project
  full-project-deployment-template/
      package.xml                        project-wide manifest; mirrors the tracker
      manual-steps.md                    manual steps for a full project cutover, if needed
  <work-item-id>-<short-name>/  one folder per work item that ships metadata
      DEPLOYMENT-RECORD.md     deployment scope, evidence, and outcome
      package.xml              that item's new and changed components
      destructiveChanges.xml   only if the item removes components
      manual-steps.md          only if the item has manual steps
  <YYYY-MM-DD>-<release-name>/ cutover plan and release notes when needed
```

- One master tracker for the whole project. Never split it per work item.
- `delivery/deployment/full-project-deployment-template/` holds the project-wide manifest and any full-cutover manual steps. Project Init must fill the verified API version before use.
- Name each work-item folder with the work item's id and a short slug from the project's tracker, for example `WI-12-account-merge`. With local tracking, that item is under root `.work-items/`.
- Keep work-item folders flat under `delivery/deployment/`. The tracker owns status.
- A manifest (`package.xml`) names the components a Salesforce CLI deploy includes.

## Step 1: update the tracker, master manifest, and work-item manifest

Do all three in the same response when any of these happens:

1. You author, modify, or rename metadata under `force-app/`.
   - Add the row if none exists, with the correct flags and Change Type. Otherwise edit the existing row.
   - A change to an existing component edits its one row. Never create a second row.
   - Add the member under the correct `<types>` block in `delivery/deployment/full-project-deployment-template/package.xml`. Refresh any member counts in its header when that header uses counts.
   - Add the member to the work item's `package.xml`.
2. The owner reports a successful deploy: set that org's flag to `Yes` for every component in the deploy.
3. You stage a component for deletion:
   - Set Change Type to `Destructive`.
   - Add it to the work item's `destructiveChanges.xml`.
   - Leave the flags showing where it is still present.
4. The owner reports a successful destructive deploy:
   - Set the affected org's flag to `No`.
   - If the component is gone from every org and from `force-app/`, delete the row and its master-manifest member.

Rules for the master manifest:
- Every CLI-deployable tracker row is a member of `delivery/deployment/full-project-deployment-template/package.xml`. Every member has a tracker row.
- A tracker row missing from the master manifest is dropped from the full-org cutover without warning.
- The master manifest is add-only. It never names a removed component.
- These rules apply to every agent and every session.

## Step 2: per-work-item manifests

- `package.xml` names only the work item's new and changed components. Its members also appear in the master manifest.
- Deploy this narrow set, not the master manifest, unless the goal is a full cutover.
- Removals go in `destructiveChanges.xml`, never in a `package.xml`.

## Step 3: types kept out of the manifest

These types cannot be deployed safely by a CLI manifest today: profiles, duplicate rules, matching rules, and compact-layout assignments. They move by change set or by hand.

- Add a tracker row for them. The tracker is the full inventory.
- Keep them out of the master manifest.
- Add their deploy as a step in the relevant `manual-steps.md`: which change set to build, which assignment to make, in what order.
- Name the exclusions in the master manifest's header comment.

Permission sets are not on this list. They get a normal tracker row and a normal manifest member. They deploy by CLI to a sandbox behind the preflight in `permissions-source-control.md`, which also decides when their flag flips.

## Step 4: manual steps (`manual-steps.md`)

Manual deploy steps live in `manual-steps.md` beside the manifest they belong to: the work item's deployment folder, or `delivery/deployment/full-project-deployment-template/` for the full cutover. A folder whose deploy needs no manual steps has no sheet.

Add a step in the same response in which you author the triggering metadata. Triggers:

- New permission set or permission set group: assign it to users.
- New field fed by an external connector: configure the connector mapping.
- New record type that needs retroactive assignment: the data update or Apex script.
- New or changed rollup: capture a pre-deploy baseline and validate the post-deploy delta.
- New scheduled Apex or scheduled flow: schedule it after the deploy.
- Migration that must clear a field before re-stamping: ordered Pre-deploy steps.
- Deploy that depends on a managed-package version, remote site setting, custom setting, or org-wide setting: a Pre-deploy verification step.
- One-time post-deploy backfill (Batch Apex, anonymous Apex, data load): a step with the full kickoff script inline.
- Any deploy where you want a pre-flight snapshot for safe rollback.

Skip the step when the deploy is self-contained:

- Pure UI or LWC changes with no permission, data, or config follow-up.
- Apex refactors that change only internal behavior.
- Formula-field changes that affect only existing in-scope data.
- Label or text-only changes.

When unsure, add the step. A step closed as "skipped" costs less than a missed action.

Step shape:

| Field | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Title | Short imperative step name. |
| Phase | `Pre-deploy`, `Deploy`, or `Post-deploy`. |
| Order | Sequence in the sheet. Use gaps of 10 (10, 20, 30). |
| Owner | Who runs the step. |
| Status | Not started, in progress, or done. |
| Body | Purpose (one or two sentences), numbered operator instructions, a verification section (SOQL, screenshot, or UI check), and inline scripts in fenced code blocks. |

- Put scripts (anonymous Apex, SOQL, CLI commands) inline in the body. Do not link to a repo file for a script that fits inline.
- Link the originating implementation task and any local work-item folder.
- The owner runs the deploys and updates each step's status.

Not in `manual-steps.md`:
- Routine steps that need no ordering.
- Work-item documentation. It lives with the work item.
- Implementation tasks. They live in the task list.
- Generic deploy commands for every Salesforce deploy.

## Tracker schema

Columns, in this fixed order:

| Column | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Component Type | Metadata type: `CustomField`, `CustomObject`, `Flow`, `ApexClass`, `ApexTrigger`, `LightningComponentBundle`, `Layout`, `FlexiPage`, `RecordType`, `QuickAction`, `PermissionSet`, `ValidationRule`, and so on. One value per row. |
| Object/Parent | Parent object for fields, layouts, record types, quick actions, validation rules. Blank for objectless types (Flow, ApexClass, LWC, PermissionSet, CustomApplication, CustomTab). |
| API Name | Full API name including any suffix. |
| Label | Label shown in Setup, or the bundle masterLabel for LWC or Aura. |
| Work Item | One link to the primary task in the project's tracker. Fall back to the work-item folder path. |
| Change Type | `New`, `Modified`, or `Destructive`. |
| Sandbox | `Yes` if deployed in the working sandbox, else `No`. Rename or add columns to match the project's orgs. |
| Production | `Yes` if deployed in production, else `No`. |
| Notes | One short current-state line: type details (`Text(255)`, `Number(18,0)`), what the component does, and any caveat (renamed-from, superseded-by, manual-step, gated-off). Use `;` instead of `,`, or quote the cell. |

## Org flags

- Flags are independent. A component can be in one org, another, or both.
- A new component not yet deployed: all flags `No`.
- When a deploy to an org lands, set that org's flag to `Yes`.
- The owner runs production deploys. When the owner reports a successful production deploy, set `Production=Yes` for its components.
- Order does not matter. `Sandbox=No, Production=Yes` is valid if that is what happened.
- Never change a flag for a failed deploy.

## Change Type

- `New`: this project created the component. Default. A created component that was later renamed is still `New`.
- `Modified`: the component existed and this project changed it. Start Notes with `Modified: ...`.
- `Destructive`: the component is being removed. Keep the row while the deletion is pending in any org. The flags mean "still present there". Delete the row once it is gone from every org and from `force-app/`.

## One row per component

- Key: Component Type + Object/Parent + API Name. One row per key.
- Renamed: keep one row under the new API name, drop the old row, note the rename in Notes.
- Replaced: keep the replacement's row and drop the replaced row, with a note. If the replaced component is still being removed, set its Change Type to `Destructive` until the deletion lands.
- Do not keep rows for components that are gone from `force-app/` and deployed nowhere. The tracker is current state. Git and the task tracker hold history.

## Project-authored only

- Track only components this project created or modified.
- Do not add components pulled into `force-app/` by a backfill or reverse-engineering snapshot. A manifest may list them; the tracker does not.
- A pre-existing component this project modified gets a row with a `Modified: ...` Notes line.

## CSV editing

- Use RFC 4180 quoting. Quote any cell with a comma, newline, or double quote. Escape `"` as `""`.
- Prefer `;` or `/` over `,` inside Notes.
- The header and column order are fixed. Ask the owner before adding a column.
- Group rows by Component Type.

## Not in the tracker

- Config changes made in the org UI with no `force-app/` file.
- Managed-package metadata this project did not author.
- Local-only files: documents, scripts, work-item folders, manifests.
- Dated deploy history. Dates live in the work log or task tracker.

## Related rules

- `check-deployment-contents.md`: reads this tracker as a hint before any deploy.
- `salesforce-org-safety.md`: what an agent may do against an org.
- `permissions-source-control.md`: how permission sets are fetched, verified, and deployed.

name: memory-save
description: 'Saves, corrects, or forgets one lasting fact in project memory, and sends anything that belongs elsewhere to its home. Use when the owner says "remember this", "from now on", "always do X", "never do X", "forget that", or "remind me", corrects the agent, or a hook says to save.'

# Memory save

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Record format, types, focus, and glossary: `references/record-format.md`. To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Put each `toolkit` command on its own line. In Codex, a `toolkit` command joined to anything else (`&&`, `;`, a pipe, a heredoc) or run from a script runs inside the sandbox, which blocks Hindsight and Notion: run it alone. Text: give it in the command with `--body "<text>"` (a save) or `--text "<text>"` (the focus or the glossary), so no file is needed. For a long text, in Claude Code pass it on standard input (`--set-file -` or `--body-file -` with a heredoc); in Codex make a new folder for each save with `mktemp -d`, write the file there, and delete the file and the folder right after the command succeeds. Never use a fixed name such as `/tmp/focus.md`: another session could write the same file.

## Steps

1. Decide the home first, with the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory; otherwise `references/record-format.md`). Memory holds a lasting preference, correction, fact about the project or the owner, or a hard-to-find reference. Elsewhere: project work goes to `work-on`; a decision for the whole project to `work-decide` (`DECISIONS.md`); delivered behavior to `requirements/`; how a change is built to the item's design; verified current structure to `system-guide/`; outside documentation to `ai-external-knowledge/`; a standing rule for how agents work here is proposed as a rule-file change; an owner to-do with no work item goes to the current focus "Untracked to-dos"; a project term goes to the glossary. A short memory pointer to a hard-to-find record is allowed; never copy its body.
2. Search first and update the existing record rather than add a duplicate.
   `toolkit memory find "<topic>"`
   `toolkit memory get <key>`
3. Approval. This is the only written copy of the memory approval policy. Read the mode, then apply it:
   `toolkit config get memory.approval`
   The owner's own words ("remember", "from now on", "always", "never", "forget", a correction) are the approval: save now, with his name as the approver. `onboarding` mode (the default): something the agent inferred gets one yes-or-no line first ("Save to memory: <one-line summary>?"); save after a yes. `trusted` mode: routine facts the agent is sure of are saved and reported, without an approver. Always ask first, in either mode, for anything about a named person, personal details, a hard delete, more than five records at once, or a change to this policy. A yes covers only the change and meaning shown. Silence is never a yes. There is no proposal inbox: keep an unanswered question in the conversation and go on with other work.
4. Save: type (`user`, `feedback`, `project`, `reference`, `event`), slug, one-line description, the source, and a body file with the model's labels: Remember, Why (the owner's reason in his words, or "Not stated by the owner."; never a reason you inferred), How to apply, Evidence and limits (the source and an absolute date), Related memories (relative links such as `[deploy window](project_deploy_window.md)`), Authoritative records. The source is the person, conversation, or document the fact came from, with an absolute date, for example "The owner, in chat, 2026-09-26" or "requirements/billing.md, 2026-09-26". Saving the same type and slug again updates that record. Replacing a record under a new name: add `--supersedes <old-key>`. Giving the same record a better name, or a type that matches its content: rename it; links to it are repaired. Use the first save form when the owner approved (his words or his yes); the second only for a routine save in `trusted` mode.
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description "<one line>" --body-file <file> --source "<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>" --approved-by <owner>`
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description "<one line>" --body-file <file> --source "<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>"`
   `toolkit memory rename <key> --to <new-key>`
5. "Forget that": retire the record (it can be undone); right after a save, retire that record with no question. Delete only when the owner says delete, and quote his words.

When a record is renamed, merged, retired, or deleted, the CLI repairs the links in other notes and names each note it changed; read that report (`references/record-format.md`, "Links between memories").
- Hindsight or Notion unreachable: the save fails with "Not saved". Keep the text, tell the owner in one line, and retry later in the session.

  `toolkit memory restore <key>`
# Local project memory

Keep future sessions oriented without turning every conversation into lasting memory. This folder is the project's built-in memory store and can be opened directly as an Obsidian vault. Active topics stay flat; filenames and YAML types agree. Git ignores this folder, so back it up with `toolkit memory export --to <folder outside this project>`.

## Read and route

- Read `CURRENT_FOCUS.md` at startup; the session briefing includes it. Read `MEMORY.md` as a short index, then open relevant topics. Check dates, scope, and the current source before acting on a remembered claim.
- Read `memory-criteria.md` before selecting or changing memory. It holds the default eligibility rules; the `memory-save` skill holds the approval policy and the onboarding or trusted mode. Use the terminology glossary for project language, including distinct meanings across systems.
- Link related notes inside this vault with relative Markdown links, such as `[account model](project_account_model.md)`. Obsidian shows backlinks to a note from the notes that link to it; a second reverse link is optional. Link only when the relationship helps retrieval, and check that the target exists. Keep tracker URLs and paths outside `.memory/` as source references rather than vault links.
- Keep current tasks and owner-mentioned to-dos in `CURRENT_FOCUS.md`, naming work items by ID. Keep full tasks, status, requirements, history, and the work item's design together in the chosen tracker; verified system behavior in the System Guide; procedures in instructions or skills; and raw outside sources in their source folders.

## Curate

- Use a coherent topic file such as `project_account_data_model.md`. Allowed prefixes and matching `metadata.type` values are `user`, `feedback`, `project`, `reference`, and `event`. `project_topic_template.md` is a seed, not a saved memory. Keep one related topic per file and aim for a quick read.
- Record source and date, status, scope, the durable point, why it matters, and how to apply it. Keep uncertainty explicit. Preserve extra YAML fields written by a host or imported record.
- Search for an existing topic before creating one (`toolkit memory find`). Correct, merge, or supersede in place where possible. Mark obsolete claims in both file text and index; do not leave an archived item reading as currently open.
- When renaming, merging, archiving, or deleting a topic, inspect links from other memory notes and repair any affected links, saving each repaired note with `toolkit memory save`. Do not leave a link pointing at a former active location.
- `toolkit memory save`, `retire`, and `restore` rebuild `MEMORY.md`; run `toolkit memory reindex` after any other topic change. The index holds one short link per active topic, not the content itself. Keep it below the configured budget.
- Keep `CURRENT_FOCUS.md` under 50 lines by replacing stale sections, not appending, and write it with `toolkit memory focus --set-file`. Do not remove an unresolved owner to-do solely to meet that limit.
- Keep the glossary broad through sourced real terms, aliases, and system-specific meanings, and write it with `toolkit memory glossary --set-file`. Do not invent definitions.

## Authority and completion

- Save through the `memory-save` skill, which holds the approval policy for onboarding and trusted mode. An explicit request to remember or correct is authorization for that specific change.
- Ask before ambiguous, bulk, or irreversible deletion of unique content. Only the owner can change the mode.
- A rejected candidate is not saved to another memory, a criteria example, the glossary, or a pending queue. Record only the general selection lesson, as a `feedback` memory, if the owner gave one.
- The main agent writes this folder only with `toolkit memory` commands (`save`, `retire`, `restore`, `delete`, `focus`, `glossary`, `reindex`). They lock the folder, refuse stale edits, and rebuild the index. Never run parallel writers against the same topic.
- Read back changes with `toolkit memory get` and run `toolkit doctor` before reporting success. Memory work does not edit requirements, work-item status, designs, deployments, or source code.
# Memory criteria

This file is the project-specific selection policy: what is worth keeping in lasting memory. The approval policy, including onboarding and trusted mode, is in the `memory-save` skill, which saves with `toolkit memory save`. When the owner corrects what is worth saving, save the correction as a `feedback` memory with `memory-save`, as a general rule, without copying the rejected memory. Those `feedback` memories override this page.

## Default test for lasting memory

Save a topic when it concerns this project, has a credible source, would matter in a future session, would be costly or unreliable to reconstruct, and has no better maintained owner. Prefer updating an existing topic. A short pointer to an authoritative record can qualify when future sessions would otherwise miss that record.

| Type and filename | Usually worth retaining | Route or reject instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `user_<topic>.md` | Relevant role, responsibility, working preference, or communication need the owner stated | Personal judgments, irrelevant biography, private details |
| `feedback_<topic>.md` | Repeated or standing correction to how the agent should work; confirmed selection lesson | One-off irritation, a rejected fact restated as policy, an instruction already in `AGENTS.md` |
| `project_<topic>.md` | Durable project constraint, rationale, technical landmark, or proven costly fix | A decision for the whole project (`DECISIONS.md`), code summary, schema copy, active ticket status, accepted requirement or design body |
| `reference_<topic>.md` | Hard-to-rediscover route to a source, system, dashboard, or decision record, with why to open it | Entire outside page or a path already obvious in `PROJECT.md` or the project map |
| `event_<topic>.md` | Significant project episode: what was done, what resulted, and where the output lives | Routine edit, tool call, raw error, daily progress log |

## Working context is different

`CURRENT_FOCUS.md` holds what is happening now: active work item IDs, what waits on the owner with no work item, untracked to-dos, and where the next session starts. It can change often. Keep a work item's detailed tasks and status in that item. Do not turn every open task into lasting memory. Do not discard an unresolved owner to-do merely to shorten the file.

## Never save as lasting memory

- Secrets, credentials, sensitive personal data, transcripts, scratch reasoning, raw logs, dropped guesses, or unsupported claims.
- A fact the same change already places in the authoritative file, unless a small route to that file is genuinely needed.
- Live status, pending approval, unshipped requirements, procedure steps, code restatements, or a current-system explanation that the code/System Guide owns.
- A rejected candidate under a new name or wider wording. A rejection stands until the owner changes it.

## Backup

This folder is Git-ignored. Back it up with `toolkit memory export --to <folder outside this project>` and restore a fresh clone with `toolkit memory import --from <that folder>`. Linked worktrees resolve to one vault in the main checkout. A fresh clone or machine needs its memory restored before the agent treats an empty index as evidence that no memory exists.

exist and not be archived); retire alone archives it (built-in: moved to

word; a superseded record stays beside the current ones.
Links to a note in other notes are repaired when it is renamed (rename, or save
--supersedes), superseded, archived (the link becomes its words plus "(archived)"),
